evidence.claim: From Lincoln’s childhood farms to the brick mansion at Federal Hill.
evidence.quote: preserving two separate farm sites in LaRue County, Kentucky, where Abraham Lincoln was born and lived early in his childhood.

evidence.claim: Old Kentucky Turnpike follows US 31E from the Abraham Lincoln birthplace through Hodgenville to Bardstown, then US 62 and US 150 to My Old Kentucky Home State Park.
evidence.quote: Beginning in Larue County on US 31E at the entrance to Abraham Lincoln Birthplace National Historic Site via Hodgenville to the Nelson County Line; then in Nelson County via Old Kentucky Turnpike 4 Larue, Nelson US 31E to Bardstown, in Bardstown via US 62 and US 150 to the entrance to My Old Kentucky Home State Park

evidence.claim: Kentucky designated this 28.059-mile scenic route on May 24, 1995.

The Federal Highway Administration describes the longer Lincoln Heritage Scenic Highway as winding through Kentucky’s knobs, linking Lincoln history, Civil War history, bourbon and religious heritage.
evidence.quote: The Lincoln Heritage Scenic Highway travels through six communities as it winds its way through the knobs of Kentucky. This corridor exhibits significant historic and cultural resources around every turn. It embraces a set of four strong aspects: Abraham Lincoln, US History and the Civil War, Bourbon Heritage, and Religious Heritage.

evidence.claim: the longer Lincoln Heritage Scenic Highway
evidence.quote: Length 71.2 mi / 114.6 km

evidence.claim: LaRue County has low rolling hills, largely cleared for agriculture or development, with wooded drainages in the east.
evidence.quote: The low rolling hills of LaRue County have been largely cleared and devoted to agriculture or urban development, with only the drainages of the eastern portions still wooded.

evidence.claim: At Knob Creek, Thomas Lincoln leased land beside the Old Cumberland Trail, now US 31E.
evidence.quote: Lincoln's father, Thomas Lincoln, leased the land by the Old Cumberland Trail (now U.S. 31E)

evidence.claim: A century later, paved roads helped turn Lincoln’s birthplace into a destination for motorists.
evidence.quote: The increase in tourism during the 1920s was due to the ease of transportation that newly paved roads for automobiles provided.

evidence.claim: The Nancy Lincoln Inn and its cabins were built in 1928 to serve those visitors.
evidence.quote: The Nancy Lincoln Inn and its cabins were built to serve the many visitors who wished to visit the birthplace of Abraham Lincoln.

evidence.claim: The Nancy Lincoln Inn and its cabins were built in 1928
evidence.quote: To the east are four small overnight cabins also built in 1928.

evidence.claim: At Knob Creek, a tavern built in 1933 also catered to the growing Lincoln tourist trade.
evidence.quote: The tavern was built to cash in on the booming tourist trade that came to LaRue County to see sites connected with Lincoln

evidence.claim: That building later became a museum and gift shop, which operated until 1998.
evidence.quote: it was converted to a museum and gift shop, as it remained until it was closed in 1998.

evidence.claim: Begin at Sinking Spring Farm’s memorial, then continue through Hodgenville, where two bronze Lincolns stand in the square, one a child and one an adult.
evidence.quote: two bronze Abraham Lincoln statues stand at the town square, one of Lincoln as a child, the other as an adult.

evidence.claim: Sinking Spring Farm’s memorial
evidence.quote: A cabin, symbolic of the one in which Lincoln was born, is preserved within a 1911 neoclassical memorial building at the site.

evidence.claim: Knob Creek Farm lies northeast of Hodgenville, near US 31E.
evidence.quote: another farm a few miles to the northeast along Knob Creek, near present-day U.S. Highway 31E

evidence.claim: At Bardstown, the route finishes at Federal Hill, the former Rowan plantation home that became My Old Kentucky Home.
evidence.quote: Federal Hill was purchased by the Commonwealth of Kentucky, dedicated as a historic site, and renamed "My Old Kentucky Home" on July 4, 1923.

evidence.claim: the former Rowan plantation home
evidence.quote: The park's centerpiece is Federal Hill, a former plantation home owned by United States Senator John Rowan

evidence.claim: Fifty-six steps lead to Lincoln’s birthplace memorial, one for each year of his life.
evidence.quote: The 56 steps leading up to the building entrance represent his age at his death.

evidence.claim: Inside is a symbolic cabin whose logs date mostly to the 1840s, rather than the building in which he was born in 1809.
evidence.quote: The Symbolic Birth Cabin represents the one Abraham Lincoln was born in on February 12, 1809. While the original was likely lost to time, the logs in this cabins date to mostly to the 1840s

evidence.claim: Architect John Russell Pope designed the neoclassical memorial; President William Howard Taft dedicated it in November 1911.
evidence.quote: A Beaux-Arts neo-classical Memorial Building was designed by John Russell Pope for the birthplace site.

evidence.claim: President William Howard Taft dedicated it in November 1911.
evidence.quote: the building was dedicated on November 9, 1911, by President William Howard Taft.

evidence.claim: The cabin proved too large for visitors to circulate easily, so the Lincoln Farm Association reduced it from sixteen by eighteen feet to twelve by seventeen.
evidence.quote: When the last rebuilt cabin was placed in the Memorial Building, its size made visitor circulation difficult. The LFA reduced the cabin's size from 16-by-18 feet to 12-by-17 feet.

evidence.claim: The memorial also uses groups of sixteen windows and ceiling rosettes to mark Lincoln’s place as the sixteenth president.
evidence.quote: The Memorial Building features 16 windows, 16 rosettes on the ceiling, and 16 fence poles, representing Lincoln being the 16th president.

evidence.claim: The memorial’s 56 entrance steps represent Lincoln’s age at death.
evidence.quote: The 56 steps leading up to the building entrance represent his age at his death.

evidence.claim: Lincoln lived at Knob Creek from age two until age seven, on land his father leased beside the Old Cumberland Trail.
evidence.quote: He was born at the Sinking Spring site south of Hodgenville and remained there until the family moved to the Knob Creek Farm northeast of Hodgenville when he was two years old, living there until he was seven years of age.

evidence.claim: on land his father leased beside the Old Cumberland Trail.
evidence.quote: Lincoln's father, Thomas Lincoln, leased the land by the Old Cumberland Trail

evidence.claim: The Lincoln family’s cabin was dismantled and its logs reused in a horse stable, later swept away by a flood.
evidence.quote: Gollaher took down the old home and used the logs to build a horse stable about a mile down the road. Years later, the stable was washed away by a flood.

evidence.claim: The Gollaher Cabin was moved here to represent what their home looked like.
evidence.quote: moved to its present location to reflect what the Lincoln cabin would look like.

evidence.claim: The other historic building, Lincoln Tavern, dates to 1933 and began as a dance hall serving the tourist trade.
evidence.quote: The Tavern was built in 1933

evidence.claim: began as a dance hall serving the tourist trade.

evidence.claim: The farm joined the national park in November 2001.
evidence.quote: The Knob Creek site was added to the National park in November 2001

evidence.claim: The family left for Indiana in December 1816, when Lincoln was almost eight.
evidence.quote: In December 1816, when Lincoln was almost eight years old, he moved with his family to a homestead in Indiana

evidence.claim: Federal Hill’s brick exterior rises above a native limestone foundation.
evidence.quote: The mansion is constructed on a native limestone foundation

evidence.quote: mansion that was planned and commissioned by Judge John Rowan and his wife Ann Lytle.

evidence.claim: whose main block was completed in 1818 using enslaved labor.

evidence.quote: A burial ground of enslaved men, women, and children is located to the southwest of the mansion

evidence.claim: The My Old Kentucky Home Commission bought the property in 1922 and gave it to Kentucky after renovation.
evidence.quote: In 1922, the "My Old Kentucky Home Commission" purchased Federal Hill from Madge Rowan Frost, the last heir of Federal Hill farm. The Commission renovated the property and gave the farm to the Commonwealth of Kentucky

Omitted the near-drowning anecdote, although it appears in the secondary cache, because no underlying account is supplied. Omitted the county dry-vote date because cache pages give 1937 and 1942.
